Determining k and Hg(II)red Purpose: To determine rate constants for reduction of mercury in Arctic snow for use in models to better predict mercury fate in hard to sample regions, or with changing climate conditions.
Snow was collected from 3 sites near Resolute Bay, NU, Canada.
A portion of the snow was melted in bottles and re-frozen for melted snow analyses.

Snow was exposed to UV radiation (25 to 250% March Arctic solar radiation) at -10°C for frozen and 4oC for 4. Inorganic mercury (Hg(II) reduced to elemental mercury (Hg(0)) was quantified (see below).

Total cumulative mercury reduced and rate constants for photoreduction were calculated, assuming pseudo-first 1. •With low UV intensity conditions (early Arctic spring), only a small amount of mercury in the snow will be lost (small Hg(II)red), but this will happen very quickly (large k).

•As the sunlit season progresses and the UV intensity increases, the rate of mercury reduction will initially decrease (low k), and then increase as the UV intensity increases (> 3 – 4 W·m-2), while the total amount of mercury reduced will increase consistently (Hg(II)red increases as UV intensity does).
•Differences in [Cl-] and [Fe] may be responsible for differences in Hg reduction behaviour between sites, seen in the Hg(II)red and k vs. UV figures.
•DOM appears to enhance/facilitate Hg reduction in frozen snow but NOT in melted snow.

Loss of DOM with irradiation - Influence on photoreducible Hg • DOM plays a different role in frozen vs. melted snow - DOM appears to enhance/allow Hg photoreduction in frozen snow  more DOM breakdown = more Hg photoreduction.
- DOM does NOT appear to enhance/allow photoreduction in melted snow; DOM may inhibit photoreduction in melted snow.
